process.title: A cold baseline paper and three counts
process.description: The student sits an unseen timed paper with no preparation, and it is marked against the published expectations. The three range counts are taken from the writing: distinct word families, longest controlled sentence, connective types. These numbers are the series everything later is compared against.

process.title: A written separation of technique from language
process.description: After the trial you receive a document that splits the losses into technique losses, which move in weeks, and language-range losses, which move across terms. For a 4EB1 student this split is the single most useful thing a tutor can produce, and it decides where every hour goes.

process.title: One error family per cycle, in clearing order
process.description: Rule-based families are attacked first because they close fast and produce visible wins. Pattern-based families follow and are tracked by falling frequency rather than closure. The correction record is open to you, and a family is closed only when it stays absent from timed work.

process.title: Counts repeated monthly, not weekly
process.description: The three range counts are retaken monthly from a timed piece and recorded on one sheet. Monthly is deliberate: a weekly count on a slow variable produces noise and tempts a plan into changing direction constantly, which is itself a common failure.

process.title: A mid-year decision point, scheduled in advance
process.description: At the midpoint the student sits an unseen paper marked identically to the baseline and the counts are repeated. If the method is working, it continues. If the counts are flat, the method changes. Sessions run one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time.

whyPoints.title: The entry question is examined first
whyPoints.description: Before hours are sold, the evidence for the Language A against Language B decision is read: section marks, band comments, error patterns and a vocabulary count. The decision stays with the school, and the evidence is what makes that conversation productive.

whyPoints.title: Range is counted, not described
whyPoints.description: Distinct word families, longest controlled sentence and connective types, taken monthly from timed work and recorded on one sheet. A parent can see movement in numbers months before it becomes audible in the writing.

whyPoints.title: Errors are tracked by family
whyPoints.description: Counting incidents tells you nothing, because a longer or braver piece produces more. Counting families tells you what to teach next and in what order, and it shows which faults have genuinely stopped under timed conditions.

whyPoints.title: Technique and language separated in writing
whyPoints.description: Task coverage, question operations, pacing and paper completion move in weeks. Vocabulary and idiom move across terms. The plan states which losses are which in week one, so hours are not spent where they cannot win.

whyPoints.title: An honest timescale for a slow variable
whyPoints.description: Language acquisition does not accelerate with intensity. Where range is the real ceiling, the plan says so, keeps the range work going and banks the technique and accuracy marks that remain available instead of selling urgency.

whyPoints.title: The student's own work stays their own
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach, question, correct and give feedback on what the student has written. Nothing is supplied for submission under a student's name, and Pearson specifications, papers and mark schemes are cited and linked rather than distributed.

faqs.question: What is Edexcel IGCSE English Language B 4EB1, and who is it for?
faqs.answer: 4EB1 is Pearson's International GCSE English Language B, designed for students working in English as an additional language. It is assessed by written examination and, unlike English Language A, carries no coursework alternative, so the whole grade rests on performance in the exam room. Confirm the current paper structure, duration and weightings on the Pearson subject page and with your child's English department, since those details are Pearson's to set and the school's to administer. The practical consequence is that progress must be measured on unseen timed work, because that is what the qualification measures.

faqs.question: Is 4EB1 easier than 4EA1?
faqs.answer: It is different rather than easier, and the framing matters because it leads families to the wrong decision. Language B assesses a student against expectations written for an additional-language learner; Language A assesses against first-language expectations. A student placed on the wrong one is disadvantaged in both directions: too high, and tuition cannot change the framing they are being judged against; too low, and a capable student is under-assessed with high marks and nothing left in the band description to criticise. Decide it on evidence from marked work, and the decision belongs to the school.

faqs.question: How do we know whether our child was entered for the right English paper?
faqs.answer: Look for a persistent pattern rather than a single result. A solid reading mark alongside a consistently lower writing mark points one way. Band comments returning repeatedly to range, idiom and expression point the same way, while comments about structure and development of ideas point the other. Systematic article, preposition and tense patterns in timed writing are evidence; occasional slips are not. Count distinct word families in one timed piece: narrow repetition of reliable words is informative. Bring the pattern to the English department in Year 9 or early Year 10, not in Year 11.

faqs.question: How is progress on 4EB1 measured when there is no coursework?
faqs.answer: On unseen timed papers, because that is what the qualification assesses, plus countable measures of range in between. The practical system is three fixed evidence points in a year: a cold baseline sat before any teaching, a mid-year paper marked identically, and a pre-mock check close enough to the school's mock window that what it reveals can still be acted on. Between those points, task coverage and paper completion are checked every piece, and the three range counts are taken monthly. No coursework means nothing accumulates towards the grade except capability.

faqs.question: How do we measure vocabulary growth rather than guess at it?
faqs.answer: Take three counts from one timed piece and repeat them monthly. Distinct word families, recorded alongside the total word count. The longest sentence the student controls accurately, in words. The number of different connectives used correctly. A real gain looks modest: word families rising from the sixties to the eighties across a term, a longest controlled sentence moving from twelve words to eighteen, four connective types becoming seven. None of that is audible in conversation and all of it eventually shows in a mark, which is exactly why counting beats sensing.

faqs.question: Which accuracy errors persist longest for an additional-language writer?
faqs.answer: Collocation and register last longest: words that are individually correct and do not belong together, or a formal word dropped into a casual sentence. Before them sit the pattern-based families, article use, preposition choice, countability and tense consistency, which take a term or more and improve by falling in frequency rather than by disappearing. Rule-based errors clear fastest, in weeks: subject-verb agreement, irregular past tenses, plurals, capitalisation. A plan should attack them in that order, because the early wins are what make the slow work bearable.

faqs.question: Do universities accept English Language B?
faqs.answer: Many do, and many ask for a separate English proficiency test instead, which is the thing to establish early. The published Ministry of Education guidance for the American track sets English proficiency at a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, which shows how commonly a test score rather than a school qualification is what gets read. Check your target universities' own requirements directly. Test preparation and 4EB1 preparation overlap only partly, so competing for the same hours is a real risk.

faqs.question: Does a 4EB1 grade count towards UAE Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: The published requirement for the British track is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level, with Arabic and Islamic education not included among the five. How a specific certificate is counted is a decision for the Ministry and the attestation authority rather than for any tutoring service. Verify your child's own case on moe.gov.ae or with the school registrar. IB Gram does not perform or influence equivalency, and tutoring is not required for it.

faqs.question: How many months before a 4EB1 grade moves?
faqs.answer: It depends which marks are being recovered, which is why the first job is to split the losses. Task coverage, question operations, pacing and paper completion are technique and commonly move within a block of six sessions, showing up on an unseen timed paper. Vocabulary range, idiom and the pattern-based accuracy families move across terms, in increments too small to notice week to week. A provider who quotes a timescale before reading a marked paper is guessing; a provider who separates the fast losses from the slow ones in week one is giving you something checkable.

faqs.question: My child reads well in English but writes poorly. What does that mean for 4EB1?
faqs.answer: It is the most common profile on this qualification and it is informative in two ways. First, it tells you the comprehension level is probably not the limiting factor, so reading-section losses are likely technique: the wrong operation performed, or general knowledge substituted for what the passage states. Second, a persistent gap between a solid reading mark and a weak writing mark is exactly the evidence worth taking to the English department when the entry decision is being discussed. Track the two separately and report them separately; combining them into one grade hides the pattern.

faqs.question: Can a 4EB1 student move up to 4EA1?
faqs.answer: It happens, and the evidence to bring is a ceiling effect: consistently high marks together with band descriptions that have nothing substantive left to criticise. A capable student held on the additional-language paper is being under-assessed, and the limitation is the framing rather than the student. Raise it with marked work and section marks in Year 9 or early Year 10, when a change is administratively manageable. The decision is the school's to make, it depends on timetabling and entry deadlines as much as on ability, and no tutoring service should present itself as the arbiter of it.

faqs.question: Does mandatory Arabic alongside English slow English progress?
faqs.answer: It occupies hours, which is a scheduling fact rather than an academic verdict. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, with KHDA requiring separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students, specified languages of instruction, and instructional time calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit. The practical consequence is that an English plan must fit the time that genuinely remains. One held weekly slot that survives the year produces far more measurable progress than three that collapse by November.

faqs.question: What evidence should a 4EB1 tutor produce each month?
faqs.answer: A short, dull, specific set: the three range counts taken from a timed piece, the list of error families still open with dates, the task-coverage record for each piece written, and a note of which single instruction is live this cycle. Plus, at the three fixed points in the year, a mark on an unseen timed paper compared with the baseline in writing, including what has not moved. None of that requires interpretation by a parent. If what arrives instead is a description of how sessions have been going, there is nothing to hold anyone to.

faqs.question: Is reading more English books enough to lift a 4EB1 grade?
faqs.answer: Reading volume genuinely helps the slow variables, particularly collocation and idiom, which are the hardest things to teach directly and the last to improve. It does nothing for the fast losses: task coverage, performing the operation a question asked, pacing, and finishing the paper. So reading is necessary and insufficient. A student who reads widely and still scores poorly is almost always losing technique marks rather than language marks, and that distinction is visible on one marked paper in about twenty minutes.

faqs.question: How do we tell whether exam technique or language level is the real limit?
faqs.answer: Read one marked paper against four checks. Did the response do everything the task asked? Did the reading answers perform the operation the question's verb named? Was the final task finished? Is the writing accurate within a narrow band of vocabulary and sentence patterns? Failing the first three is technique, which moves in weeks. Passing all three while the fourth is true means the range is genuinely the ceiling, and the honest plan then keeps range work going and banks the remaining technique and accuracy marks rather than selling intensity.

dubai/edexcel-igcse-english-language-b-4.closingBody: The hardest thing about this qualification is that real progress is invisible for weeks at a time, which makes a measurement system worth more than any promise. Send one marked timed piece with its band description and the section marks if the school publishes them. Take the free trial as a cold baseline: an unseen paper, no preparation, marked against the published expectations, with the three range counts taken from the writing. What comes back is a written split of the losses into technique, which moves in weeks, and range, which moves across terms, plus the error families in clearing order. If that document says the entry itself should be discussed with the school first, it will say so. Sessions run one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time.

dubai/edexcel-igcse-english-literature-4.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Literature to Years 10 and 11. Sessions run over live video on Gulf Standard Time, built around the texts your child's Dubai school has chosen, with written work marked between lessons and returned to you.

intro.heading: The honest answer to a home-tutor search, before anything else
paragraphs: Start with the thing most pages in this market bury. IB Gram does not make home visits in Dubai, or anywhere else in the UAE. Home visiting is a service we run only in India. Every lesson we deliver to a Dubai family happens one-to-one over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time. If what you need is a person at the door, this is the wrong page, and you have not wasted twenty minutes finding that out.

The reason the phrase is still in the heading is that it is what parents type. 'Home tutor' in Dubai has drifted away from its literal meaning: for a great many families it now means private, one-to-one, outside school, at home — and the question of whether the tutor physically travels is secondary to whether the hour is any good. Rather than pretend otherwise, this page treats the in-home option as a real alternative, prices it with published sources, and sets out where each format wins. You can then decide, which is more useful than being sold to.

There is a second reason the format question matters more for English Literature than for most subjects. Literature tuition is text work. The student's essay, the examiner's published criteria and the poem all need to be visible at once, and the useful part of the hour is watching a paragraph get rebuilt. Two people at a kitchen table share one piece of paper and one pen. On screen, a paragraph can be annotated live in colour, the criteria can sit beside it, and the marked version is a file the parent opens later. Several of the things families assume they lose by going online are things that only work online.

The third factor is the pool. A Dubai family hiring in-home is choosing from English teachers willing to drive to their community at a particular hour on a particular evening. That is a short list, and it is defined by road geography rather than by who has taught Pearson 4ET1. For a specific code, with a specific set-text combination chosen by one school's English department, the difference between those two lists is the difference between a tutor who knows the anthology selection and a tutor who will meet it for the first time in your lesson.

What follows is the detail: market rates with attribution, a format comparison for text-based subjects specifically, how shared annotation actually works, what a Dubai evening realistically allows, what a parent should receive each week, the permit position under UAE law, and what we say when no 4ET1 specialist is free. Nothing here promises a tutor at a Dubai address, because nobody will be arriving at one. Read the rate table, read the format comparison, and then choose.

dubai/edexcel-igcse-english-literature-4.programmesIntro: Which programme a student sits changes what a weekly English session has to carry. These are the routes behind the Year 10 and Year 11 students Dubai families ask us about, framed around what each one does to a home-tuition timetable.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Literature
programmes.description: Graded 9-1 and assessed on poetry, modern prose, modern drama and literary heritage texts, with an unseen poem and a coursework route available at centres that enter it. Text choices are made school by school from the specification menu, so the preparation is only transferable between students at the same school.
programmes.countryNote: The scheduling consequence in Dubai is that written work has to happen between sessions, not inside them. An hour spent reading a chapter aloud is an hour not spent on the paragraph that lost marks. Families who protect thirty minutes of writing time midweek get roughly double the value from the same fee.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Language A
programmes.description: Non-fiction reading plus transactional and imaginative writing. Sat alongside Literature by most Dubai students and usually taught by the same teacher, which is why weak Literature marks often get treated as a general English problem and answered with more writing practice.
programmes.countryNote: For a family budgeting hours, the useful move is to decide which of the two is actually dropping marks before buying a term. One marked baseline piece in each takes a week and frequently halves the number of hours needed, because only one of the two usually needs attention.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme, Years 4 and 5
programmes.description: Assessed against criteria A to D with no terminal written paper. Students who move into a 4ET1 class from an MYP school in Dubai meet closed-text timed essay writing late, and the first obstacle is almost always the clock rather than the reading.
programmes.countryNote: Mid-phase school moves are common in this city, and families often book tuition in the term after the move. Where that is the situation, the first block should be timing and planning drills, which need a stopwatch and a screen rather than a visitor in the living room.

programmes.name: A Level English Literature and IB Diploma Language A
programmes.description: The two continuation routes after 16 at Dubai schools. Both assume the analytical habit 4ET1 is supposed to install, and both punish a student who reached a good IGCSE grade by memorising essays rather than writing them under pressure.
programmes.countryNote: If sixth form is the reason for booking now, the honest brief is different: fewer hours, aimed at method rather than content, finishing well before the series. That plan is cheaper than a crisis block in April and it survives the move into Year 12.

dubai/edexcel-igcse-english-literature-4.subjectsIntro: Families booking English Literature usually ask about one or two more subjects in the same message, because Dubai option blocks group the essay subjects and because one tutor cannot sensibly cover everything. These are the codes most often requested alongside 4ET1.

subjects.name: English Literature (4ET1)
subjects.description: The subject this page covers. Weekly work is a timed response written between sessions, marked against the published criteria, with the lesson spent rebuilding the sentences that lost marks rather than discussing the plot.

subjects.name: English Language A (4EA1)
subjects.description: Form and audience are where marks go: a student writes an essay when the task asked for a speech. Short, frequent writing tasks suit this better than long sessions, which is a scheduling point as much as a teaching one.

subjects.name: English Language B (4EB1)
subjects.description: The route for students working in English as an additional language, used by several Dubai schools for recent arrivals. Accuracy and task completion drive the marks, and progress is quick enough to be visible inside a term.

subjects.name: History (4HI1)
subjects.description: Source handling and extended writing. Shares the evidence-and-argument habit with Literature, so students sometimes make faster progress in History once the Literature sentence pattern has landed.

subjects.name: Geography (4GE1)
subjects.description: Physical and human topics with a fieldwork investigation. Command words are stricter than in Literature and the answers shorter, which suits students who find long essays exhausting.

subjects.name: Economics (4EC1)
subjects.description: Micro, business economics, macro and the global economy. The final evaluation sentence carries more marks than the preceding paragraphs and is the part most often left unwritten when time runs out.

subjects.name: Business (4BS1)
subjects.description: Case-study stimulus across enterprise, people, finance, marketing and operations. Strong readers do well once they learn to use the firm in the stimulus instead of answering in general terms.

subjects.name: Mathematics A (4MA1)
subjects.description: Tiered, and the tier carries a grade ceiling. Worth confirming in Year 10 which tier the school has entered, because discovering it in Year 11 removes options a family would have wanted.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Required alongside the licensed curriculum in all Dubai private schools. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, which is timetable arithmetic worth knowing before adding tuition hours.

sections.heading: What a Dubai family is actually buying when they search for a home tutor
paragraphs: Three different purchases hide behind the same phrase. The first is convenience: nobody has to drive anywhere, and the hour sits inside an evening that is already full. The second is attention: one adult, one child, no set of twenty-five, with the work the school cannot mark in detail getting marked. The third is reassurance: a parent in the next room, able to hear whether the hour is any good. Those three are worth separating, because only the first of them actually requires a person to travel.

Convenience survives the move online intact, and improves in one specific way. A visit has a start time set by traffic, which in Dubai means a fifteen-minute uncertainty band on Al Khail Road or Sheikh Zayed Road at six in the evening. A video session starts when it says it will. Nobody is let into the building, nobody needs the guest parking code, and a session during half-term travel or school exam leave happens anyway rather than being cancelled.

Attention survives too, and this is where English Literature differs from, say, early-years phonics. The thing being taught is a sentence on a page. Both people need to see the same sentence and be able to write on it. A shared screen does that better than a shared sheet of paper, because two cursors can work at once, the published criteria sit alongside, and the result is saved rather than folded into a school bag. For a subject assessed by handwritten essay, the preparation is still handwritten — but the review of it works better on a screen.

Reassurance is the one that changes shape, and it changes for the better if the service is set up for it. A parent in the room during a visit hears tone and can tell whether their child is engaged. A parent reading a marked script and a session note can see which sentences gained marks and which did not. The second is harder evidence than the first. Families who have had both usually say the paperwork told them more than the overheard conversation did, and it is the thing to insist on whichever format you choose.

sections.heading: The in-home English tuition market in Dubai: rates, travel and who is free on a Tuesday
paragraphs: Published pricing is thin in this market. Of the agencies competing for these searches, several publish no hourly figure at all and two quote in US dollars, which is not a currency Dubai families transact in. The bands below are market rates taken from providers' own published pricing and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table. They describe the market, not an IB Gram price list, and they are here so a parent can judge whether a quote is normal before accepting it.

In-home one-to-one in Dubai, travel included, runs roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour. Bestimate's band is AED 180 to 350; independent home tutors advertise up to AED 500. Monthly in-home packages of four two-hour sessions appear at AED 1,599 to AED 1,799. Online, a qualified subject teacher sits between about AED 150 and AED 300, with Unitors advertising IGCSE tuition from AED 150, and budget online provision runs from AED 45 to AED 150, with EdFlik from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. Subject specialists at IGCSE and A Level are AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase at AED 270, and premium named tutors reach AED 650 at BartyED.

The number the rate card hides is travel. A tutor crossing from Mirdif to Town Square in the evening spends more than an hour in a car for a one-hour booking. That time is paid for by someone, either as a visibly higher rate or as a tutor who takes only the three communities nearest home. Both outcomes shrink the pool a specific family can choose from, and for a niche code like 4ET1 with a school-specific text list, the pool is the thing that matters most. Ask any in-home provider two questions: how far is the tutor travelling, and how many English teachers who have taught this specification are willing to make that drive on a Tuesday at six.

One more piece of context for a tuition budget. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package. For most families the live question is not whether tuition is affordable in principle but how few hours can be made to do the job. One hour a week with full marking included generally outperforms three unmarked hours bought in panic in April.

sections.heading: Online against in-home for a text-based subject specifically
paragraphs: Generic comparisons of online and in-home tutoring are not much help, because the answer differs by subject. A six-year-old learning to form letters needs a hand next to theirs. A sixteen-year-old being taught to rebuild an analytical sentence needs the sentence visible, editable and saved. English Literature sits firmly at the second end, and the comparison below is written for that case rather than for tutoring in general.

The practical advantages of the screen are mostly about the artefact. A paragraph can be annotated live in two colours while the student watches it change, which is the single most useful minute in a literature lesson. The published assessment criteria can sit open beside the student's own sentence, so the judgement is visible rather than asserted. The marked version becomes a file the parent opens that evening and the student revisits in April. None of that happens with one annotated printout that goes home in a bag.

In-home holds genuine advantages, and it is worth naming them rather than pretending otherwise. A tutor in the room can see a student disengage three minutes before it shows on a screen. Physical texts can be laid out side by side and flicked through faster than files. For a student who will not stay off their phone without an adult present, presence is leverage. Those are real, and a family that needs them should buy in-home and should expect to pay the travel.

What families should not accept in either format is an unmarked hour. The expensive part of literature tuition is the thirty to forty minutes a tutor spends marking a full timed essay outside the lesson, and it is the part that moves a grade. A visit at AED 300 with no marking is worse value than an online hour at AED 200 with marking included. Ask the question in the first conversation, in those words, and compare the answers rather than the hourly rates.

sections.heading: The annotated copy problem, and how a shared text actually works
paragraphs: The objection families raise most often is about the book. A literature student annotates their copy over months: margin notes, underlining, a shorthand only they understand. The worry is that an online tutor cannot see any of it, and that the lesson becomes two people discussing a text neither can point at. It is a fair objection and it has a mechanical answer.

Your child keeps their physical copy and keeps annotating it, because that is where revision lives and because the examination is sat with a pen. What moves to the screen is a shared working document: the quotations currently in play, typed out with space underneath, plus the student's own paragraphs. When the tutor asks for the line about the room in chapter nine, the student reads it from their book and types the fragment into the shared file. That act alone does useful work, because choosing which three words to type is the analytical decision most students skip.

The shared file then becomes the thing the course of study is built on. It accumulates a quotation bank the student has selected and justified, rather than one copied from a revision guide. Paragraphs get rebuilt in it, with the earlier version left visible underneath so the improvement is legible to a parent who was not in the room. Before a mock, the student has a document containing every sentence pattern they have been taught, in their own words, about their own texts. Nothing in a pile of marked printouts does that.

For poetry the mechanics differ slightly. Anthology poems are typed into the shared file once and annotated collaboratively across the term, with colour used consistently: one colour for structural observations, one for language, one for effect. Students who struggle to start an essay often discover that the colour coding has already produced the plan. Unseen poems are handled differently again, on a blank page with a stopwatch, because the point there is procedure under pressure rather than accumulated annotation.

sections.heading: Reading aloud, and the student who says they hate reading
paragraphs: A fair proportion of the 4ET1 students we meet in Dubai do not enjoy reading, and families treat this as the root problem to be solved before anything else can improve. It is usually better understood as a separate issue that need not be solved first. A student who finds reading effortful can still be taught to write high-scoring analysis, because the analysis is performed on short extracts, not on the experience of having loved the book.

Reading aloud still has a place, and it works on video without difficulty. Hearing a student read a paragraph tells a tutor several things quickly: whether the syntax of older literary heritage language is landing, where they stop understanding, and whether they are skimming past the words that carry the meaning. Three minutes of reading aloud at the start of a session is diagnostic, not remedial, and students accept it more readily when told why it is happening.

The thing that actually changes attitude is competence arriving. A student who has written one paragraph that was praised for a specific reason will write a second. We get there by narrowing the task until success is likely: not 'write about the theme of isolation' but 'write two sentences about why that one word is repeated'. Small, specific, achievable, then built up. Parents sometimes find this frustrating in week two and persuasive in week six, which is roughly the right order.

What we do not do is promise a child will come to love literature. Some do; plenty go on to good grades without it, and framing the subject as a personality transformation puts pressure on a student who already feels judged. The honest target is a method they can execute under exam conditions on a text they are indifferent to. That is achievable, it is measurable, and it does not require anyone to pretend.

sections.heading: What a weekly session should be doing in Year 10, and what changes in Year 11
paragraphs: Families often buy the same hour for two years and wonder why the return tails off. The subject does not need the same lesson throughout. Year 10 is for installing the sentence patterns and reading the texts to the end; Year 11 is for timing, question focus and the unseen procedure; the final weeks are for full papers and nothing else. A plan that ignores this spends September on exam technique a student cannot yet execute and April on close reading that is no longer the bottleneck.

There is also a sequencing point specific to Literature. Analysis cannot start while the student is still finding out what happens. A student halfway through a novel is working with incomplete information, and asking them to write about structure is asking them to guess. The early job is therefore reading pace, and it is worth being blunt with a Year 10 who is three chapters behind: the tuition cannot do its work until the book is finished.

The table below sets out the shape most of our Dubai 4ET1 students follow, with what should be written between sessions at each stage. The stage boundaries move for a November resit candidate, where everything compresses and the pre-series block comes early. For a student sitting May/June in Year 11, this is roughly it.

One scheduling note. The two periods when families most want to add hours — mock season and the fortnight before the series — are the two when the student has least capacity to use them. Mocks are more useful as data than as a reason to double up, and the final fortnight should be lighter, not heavier. We would rather move hours forward into the autumn than sell them in April.

sections.heading: The Dubai evening: school runs, activities, Ramadan and exam leave
paragraphs: The reason home tutoring is searched for so heavily in this city is the shape of the day. School buses leave early and return late, the gap between arriving home and dinner is short, and most Year 10 and 11 students have at least two fixed commitments in the week. A tutoring slot has to fit a real evening, and the commonest cause of a failed arrangement is not a bad tutor but a slot that was never going to hold.

Our practical advice is to pick the slot for the worst week, not the best one. A 4.30pm start works in October and collapses in November when the bus is late twice. A 7pm or 7.30pm start survives, and a student who is tired at 7pm is still more use than a student who is not there at 4.30pm. Families in the outer communities — Town Square, Nad Al Sheba, Al Furjan — should assume the later end. Families in Motor City or Sports City, where school and home sit in the same community, can often hold an earlier slot.

Ramadan changes the week rather than suspending it, and the standard adjustment is to move sessions to post-Iftar timing for the month. That is normal and we plan for it rather than treating it as a disruption; it is also a period when short, focused half-hour sessions outperform full hours. School exam leave and family travel are the other two predictable interruptions, and online delivery handles both, because a session can run from a hotel room if the connection holds.

The one period we recommend protecting absolutely is the month either side of the mocks. Not by adding hours, but by not cancelling the ones already booked: it is the stretch where the marked evidence is most useful and where a student's own sense of where they stand is least reliable. Everything else in the year can bend.

sections.heading: What you should receive each week, and the permit question asked properly
paragraphs: A family paying AED 200 or more an hour should be receiving documents, not impressions. After each session, expect a short written note: what was covered, what the student is writing before next time, and one specific thing they are now doing differently. After each piece of written work, expect the marked script, annotated against the published criteria. Monthly, expect a one-paragraph view of whether the plan is working. If none of that arrives, the honest reading is that the hour is a conversation, and conversations do not move grades.

On the legal side, private tutoring in the UAE runs under a permit regime that parents are entitled to ask about. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible categories include teachers employed in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so treat any specific figure quoted at you as unverified. The official application route is MoHRE's own private tutor licensing service.

Two related points are worth knowing. In Abu Dhabi, ADEK's professional-ethics rules bar private and charter school staff from paid tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct carries a similar restriction — so 'your child's own teacher, privately' is not an arrangement to go looking for. And a tutoring operation with premises and staff in Dubai is a different legal animal from an individual tutor: that requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute. IB Gram does not hold one, does not operate premises in the UAE, and does not describe itself in those terms.

On data, a tuition enquiry about a child involves personal information, and UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection governs it. We collect the student's year group, school, board, subject codes and the parent's contact details, because matching is impossible without them. We do not need a child's photograph, grades history or report cards to match a tutor, and a provider asking for them should be asked why. Deletion can be requested at any time.

sections.heading: If no 4ET1 specialist is free: what we say instead of yes
paragraphs: No competitor in this market discloses a coverage limit, which is strange, because every matching service has one. 4ET1 with a specific school's text combination is a narrow brief, and there are weeks when nobody suitable has a free slot at the hour a family needs. The useful thing a service can do at that point is say so.

What we do is offer the alternatives explicitly and let the family choose. Sometimes that is a different hour with the right tutor, which is usually the best of the options and the one families resist. Sometimes it is a tutor who teaches the Cambridge equivalent rather than Pearson, which is workable for sentence-level method and the unseen procedure but not for set-text knowledge, and we say which parts transfer. Sometimes it is a short wait with a date attached. Occasionally it is none of those, and the honest answer is that we cannot help this term.

What we will not do is place a general English tutor on a 4ET1 brief and let a family find out in week four. That costs more than the delay, because a term spent on the wrong text or the wrong skill cannot be recovered in Year 11. It is also the specific failure that produces the complaint every tutoring service receives most often, and it is almost always a matching decision made to avoid saying no.

The practical consequence for a parent is that the first conversation should end with a named tutor, a confirmed hour and a confirmed text list, or with a clear statement that one of those is missing and when it will be resolved. A booking that is vague about any of the three is not yet a booking. Ask which of the three is settled before paying anything.

faqs.question: Can we get an Edexcel IGCSE English Literature home tutor in Dubai?
faqs.answer: In-home tutoring exists in Dubai and the market rate, travel included, runs roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour on Bestimate's 2026 figures and independent home tutors' own pricing. IB Gram is not one of those providers: we do not make home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE, because home visiting is a service we run only in India. What we deliver to Dubai families is the same one-to-one help over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with written work marked between sessions. If you specifically need a person in the room, buy in-home and expect to pay the travel.

faqs.question: How much do in-home English tutors charge in Dubai per hour?
faqs.answer: Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350, and independently advertised home tutors reach AED 500. Monthly in-home packages of four two-hour sessions appear at AED 1,599 to 1,799. Online, qualified subject teachers sit at AED 150 to 300, specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above, and budget provision from AED 45. Those are market figures from the providers that publish them, not our price list. The question worth asking alongside the rate is whether full written marking of timed essays is included, because that is the part that moves a grade.

faqs.question: How does annotating a novel work if the lesson is on video?
faqs.answer: Your child keeps their physical copy and keeps annotating it, since the exam is sat with a pen. A shared document holds the working material: quotations the student has typed out themselves, with space underneath for analysis, and their paragraphs with earlier versions left visible beneath the rebuilt ones. Typing a three-word fragment is itself the analytical decision most students skip, so the mechanics do useful teaching. By mock season the file is a revision document in the student's own words, which a pile of annotated printouts never becomes.

faqs.question: Which is better for a literature subject, a home tutor or an online tutor?
faqs.answer: For English Literature the screen has a specific advantage: the student's own paragraph can be annotated live in colour with the published criteria open beside it, and the marked version becomes a file you keep. In-home has real advantages too — a tutor in the room spots disengagement faster, and presence is leverage with a student who will not leave their phone alone. The decisive factor is usually the pool. Online lets you choose a teacher of the 4ET1 specification; in-home lets you choose from those willing to drive to your community on a Tuesday.

faqs.question: What time can a 4ET1 session start on a Dubai school night?
faqs.answer: Choose the slot that survives your worst week, not your best one. A 4.30pm start works in October and fails in November when the bus runs late twice. Families in Motor City or Sports City, where school and home share a community, often hold an earlier slot. Families in Town Square, Nad Al Sheba or Al Furjan should assume 6.30pm or later. A tired student at 7pm is more use than an absent one at 4.30pm, and a slot that collapses twice usually ends the arrangement altogether.

faqs.question: Does my child need a physical copy of the set text for online lessons?
faqs.answer: Yes, and they should keep annotating it. The exam is handwritten and revision happens in the margins of a book a student knows their way around. The shared file online is not a replacement for that copy; it holds the selected quotations, the rebuilt paragraphs and the anthology poems being annotated collaboratively. We do not supply texts, specifications, past papers or mark schemes as downloads — those are published documents we cite and link rather than reproduce, and a tutor offering a private library of them is a reason for caution.

faqs.question: How many weeks before the English Literature exam should we start?
faqs.answer: Earlier than most families do, and for a different reason than they expect. Analysis cannot begin while a student is still discovering how a text ends, so the first job is finishing the reading. A student three chapters behind in March is not ready for exam technique in April. A realistic shape is sentence patterns through Year 10, full timed essays through the autumn of Year 11, the unseen procedure six to ten weeks out, and full papers in the final six weeks. A four-week block in April is salvage work, and we will say so.

faqs.question: What should a weekly 4ET1 session cover in Year 10 as opposed to Year 11?
faqs.answer: Year 10 is for reading pace and installing sentence patterns, with short pieces written between sessions. Year 11 moves to full timed essays, question focus and quotation handling, then to the unseen procedure and timing drills six to ten weeks out, then to whole papers. Buying the same hour for two years is why the return tails off. The two periods families most want to add hours — mock season and the last fortnight — are the two when a student can least use them, so we move hours forward rather than selling them in April.

faqs.question: Can two siblings share one English Literature session?
faqs.answer: Only if they are in the same year at the same school and therefore on the same text list, which rules out most sibling pairs. Where it does apply, a paired hour works and costs each family less, but it is harder for the tutor and only suits students within about a grade of each other. We decline it more often than we agree to it, because a wide attainment gap means one of the two is being carried. Written work is still marked individually, and we cap pairs at two students rather than running a class.

faqs.question: Do private English tutors in Dubai need a MoHRE permit?
faqs.answer: Private tutoring in the UAE operates under a permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The MoHRE private tuition work permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible categories include school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so treat any figure quoted at you as unverified. The official route is MoHRE's private tutor licensing service page.

faqs.question: What happens to our English Literature session during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Sessions normally move to post-Iftar timing for the month, which we plan for rather than treat as a disruption. It is also a period where two shorter focused sessions often work better than one full hour, particularly for a student fasting through a school day. Fixed weekly slots are re-agreed for the month and then returned to the original time afterwards. School exam leave and family travel are the other predictable interruptions in a Dubai year, and online delivery handles both, since a session can run from anywhere with a usable connection.

faqs.question: Can my child read aloud to a tutor over video?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is worth doing for about three minutes at the start of a session. Hearing a student read tells a tutor whether older literary heritage syntax is landing, where comprehension stops, and whether they are skimming past the words carrying the meaning. It is diagnostic rather than remedial, and students cooperate more readily when told why it is happening. It is not a substitute for written work, which is where the marks are decided and where the marking time goes.

faqs.question: What should I receive after each 4ET1 session?
faqs.answer: A short written note saying what was covered, what the student is writing before the next lesson, and one specific thing they are now doing differently. Alongside it, the marked script for the last piece of written work, annotated against the published criteria. Monthly, a paragraph on whether the plan is working. If none of that arrives, the hour is a conversation rather than tuition, whatever the format. Ask for this in the first week rather than in month three, when a term has already gone.

faqs.question: My child says they hate reading. Can a tutor change that in a year?
faqs.answer: Possibly, but it is not the target and treating it as one puts pressure on a student who already feels judged. A student who finds reading effortful can still be taught to write high-scoring analysis, because the analysis happens on short extracts rather than on having loved the book. What changes attitude is competence arriving: a narrowed task, a paragraph that worked, a specific reason it worked. Parents often find that approach frustrating in week two and persuasive in week six, which is roughly the right order.

faqs.question: Can we pause lessons during school exam leave in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Yes, and sometimes you should. The period we advise against pausing is the month either side of the mocks, not because hours should be added but because that is when marked evidence is most useful and a student's own sense of where they stand is least reliable. Everything else in the year can bend. Online delivery also means a session during exam leave or family travel can simply happen from wherever your child is, which removes most of the reason to pause in the first place.

faqs.question: How quickly can a 4ET1 tutor be matched for a Dubai family?
faqs.answer: With the code, the school's text list and a workable evening slot, usually within a few days. Without them, longer, because the first session gets spent finding out what should have been in the first email. There are weeks when nobody who teaches this specification is free at the hour you need, and we say so rather than placing a general English tutor on the brief. In that situation the options are a different hour, a short wait with a date attached, or an honest no for the term.

An hour with a full timed essay marked against the published criteria moves a grade; an hour of discussion does not, in anyone's living room. Send us the specification code, the school's set texts and the evening slot that survives a bad week. Take a trial lesson at no charge, with no card details required, and ask whichever provider you are weighing up whether marking is inside their rate. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

dubai/edexcel-igcse-english-literature-4.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Literature at Years 10 and 11. Each works from the set texts a Dubai school has chosen, marks timed essays against the published criteria, and returns the script with the marks shown where they were won and lost.

intro.heading: Why a well-read Year 11 can still sit at grade 5 in 4ET1
paragraphs: English Literature is the subject where effort and outcome come apart most visibly. A student can finish every set text, highlight half the pages, sit down in the exam hall and still write an answer that earns a middling mark. Parents in Dubai see this and reasonably conclude that more reading is the answer. It rarely is. The reading is usually fine. What is missing is the particular kind of writing Pearson rewards, which almost nobody is taught explicitly and which has very little to do with liking books.

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Literature carries the specification code 4ET1. Under the current specification it is assessed by written examination covering poetry, modern prose, modern drama and literary heritage texts, with a coursework route available at centres that choose to enter it instead of the second written paper. The live specification on qualifications.pearson.com gives the components, durations and weightings, and your child's head of English confirms which route the school has entered. That single question — which route — changes a revision plan completely, and a surprising number of families have never asked it.

What the examiner is paid to find is a student writing about how a writer has made something happen on the page. Not what happens in the story. Not how the poem made the reader feel. How the text is built, and what the building does. A sentence that says 'the writer uses a simile here' earns nothing on its own, because it describes the furniture rather than the room. A sentence that says what the comparison forces the reader to hold in mind at that exact moment in the scene is doing the work the mark scheme describes. The gap between those two sentences is most of the grade.

Dubai adds its own complications. Most of the city's British-curriculum schools run large Year 11 cohorts, which means English sets of twenty-five or more and an English teacher marking perhaps a hundred and fifty full essays a term. Detailed written feedback on every draft is arithmetically impossible, however good the department. A student who needs to see their own sentence rebuilt three times before the method sticks will not get that in class. They will get a grade, a comment and the next text. This is the specific hole that one-to-one tuition fills, and it is why the request usually arrives in January rather than September.

A 4ET1 tutor working properly spends the first session reading, not teaching. One timed essay on a text the student has already studied, marked against the published criteria, annotated so that the parent can see which sentences earned marks and which were simply true. From there the plan writes itself: a student losing marks on quotation handling needs a different term to one losing them on question focus or on running out of time on the second question. Both look like 'needs help with English' from the outside. They need opposite lessons.

dubai/edexcel-igcse-english-literature-4.programmesIntro: 4ET1 sits inside a wider set of qualifications Dubai schools run at 16, and the route a student is on changes what a literature session has to do. These are the programmes that produce English Literature students in this city, and what each one means for tuition.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Literature
programmes.description: The qualification this page is about, graded 9-1 and assessed by written examination on poetry, modern prose, modern drama and literary heritage texts. Centres may enter a coursework route in place of one written paper. The specification sets the texts available; each school picks its own combination, so two Dubai students sitting 4ET1 in the same series may share no text at all.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai centres can enter either the May/June or the November series, and both are used here: November is where resits and private candidates cluster. Because the set texts are chosen school by school, the first thing a Dubai tutor establishes is the exact title list, including which anthology poems the department has prioritised. Guessing wastes a term.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Language A
programmes.description: The companion qualification most 4ET1 students sit alongside Literature. It tests reading of non-fiction and transactional and imaginative writing rather than textual analysis of set works. The skills overlap less than parents assume: a student can be comfortable in Language A and still write weak Literature answers, because the questions ask for different things.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the two are usually timetabled with the same teacher, which is why a Literature problem often gets diagnosed as an English problem and treated with general writing practice. Separating them matters. A tutor who confirms which paper the marks are actually dropping on avoids a term of work on the wrong skill.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme, Years 4 and 5
programmes.description: The alternative route at 16 in Dubai's IB schools. MYP Language and Literature assesses against criteria A to D with no terminal written examination, so students arriving into a 4ET1 class from an MYP school meet timed closed-text essay writing for the first time quite late.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai has enough mid-phase school moves that this transition shows up every year, usually as a strong reader who cannot finish in time. The fix is mechanical rather than literary: planning in four minutes, writing to a clock, and learning how much a hand can actually produce in the time the paper allows.

programmes.name: A Level English Literature and IB Diploma Language A
programmes.description: Where a 4ET1 student goes next if the subject continues. Both demand sustained independent argument across longer texts, and both assume the analytical habit 4ET1 is meant to establish. Students who reached grade 7 at 16 by memorising essays rather than writing them find the first term of either course unpleasant.
programmes.countryNote: Most Dubai British-curriculum schools split at 16 into A Level or the IB Diploma, and the English choice is often made on which teacher the student liked. A session or two spent on what each course actually assesses is a better basis for that decision than a conversation at an options evening.

dubai/edexcel-igcse-english-literature-4.subjectsIntro: Families who come to us for 4ET1 usually ask about a second subject in the same conversation, because option blocks in Dubai schools cluster the essay subjects together. These are the Pearson codes most often requested alongside English Literature.

subjects.name: English Literature (4ET1)
subjects.description: Poetry, modern prose, modern drama and literary heritage texts. Marks are lost on method rather than knowledge: feature-spotting instead of analysis, quotation dropped in rather than built into a sentence, and answers that describe the plot of a text the examiner already knows.

subjects.name: English Language A (4EA1)
subjects.description: Non-fiction reading plus transactional and imaginative writing. The common failure is register: a student writes a competent essay when the question asked for a speech or a letter, and loses form marks that had nothing to do with the quality of the prose.

subjects.name: English Language B (4EB1)
subjects.description: The route for students working in English as an additional language, with listening, reading and writing components. Used by several Dubai schools for recent arrivals. Tuition here is about accuracy and task completion rather than literary analysis.

subjects.name: History (4HI1)
subjects.description: Source handling and extended writing on depth studies and investigations. Students who write strong Literature essays often transfer well, because both reward a claim supported by evidence that is then weighed rather than simply listed.

subjects.name: Geography (4GE1)
subjects.description: Physical and human geography with fieldwork investigation. The written demand is shorter than Literature but the command words are stricter, and marks go missing when a student explains a process without ever naming the place the question specified.

subjects.name: Economics (4EC1)
subjects.description: Microeconomics, business economics, macroeconomics and the global economy. The evaluation sentence at the end of the long question is worth more than the three paragraphs above it, and is the part students most often leave unwritten.

subjects.name: Business (4BS1)
subjects.description: Enterprise, people, finance, marketing and operations, assessed through case-study stimulus. A strong Literature student usually reads the stimulus well, then forgets to use it, writing a general answer when the marks sit in applying theory to the firm described.

subjects.name: Mathematics A (4MA1)
subjects.description: Tiered, which matters: the Foundation tier carries a grade ceiling, so the tier a Dubai school has entered a student for is worth confirming in Year 10 rather than discovering in Year 11.

subjects.name: Biology (4BI1)
subjects.description: Two written papers with practical skills assessed in writing rather than in a lab. The extended-response questions reward structured explanation, which is exactly the habit a Literature tutor builds, applied to a different content set.

subjects.name: Chemistry (4CH1)
subjects.description: Principles, inorganic, physical and organic chemistry across two papers. Requested alongside Literature by students keeping a science-plus-humanities mix open for A Level choices at 16.

sections.heading: What 4ET1 actually asks a sixteen-year-old to do
paragraphs: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Literature asks for one thing in several costumes: an argument about how a text works, supported by evidence from the text, written under time pressure. Everything else on the paper is a variation on that. The poetry questions ask it about compressed language. The prose and drama questions ask it across a longer narrative. The unseen element asks it about a text the student has never read. The underlying demand does not change between them, which is why a student who learns it once tends to improve across the whole paper rather than in one section.

The demand is unusual because it is not a knowledge test. A student can know a novel intimately and score poorly, which feels unjust and is the source of most of the frustration families bring to a first session. The examiner is not checking whether the book was read. They are checking whether the student can take a specific choice the writer made — a word, a structural decision, a pattern of imagery across two chapters — and say what that choice does to a reader. Knowledge of the plot is the floor, not the answer.

This is also what makes the subject teachable in a way parents often doubt. Analysis is not a personality trait. It is a set of sentence moves that can be named, practised and checked. A student who writes 'this shows the character is lonely' can be taught, in about four sessions, to write 'the repetition of the same room across three chapters leaves the reader with nowhere else to look, which is the point the writer is making about her choices'. Same reading, same text, a different grade band. What changes is the shape of the sentence, and sentence shapes are learnable.

The final piece is time. The paper is written by hand under a clock, and a student who plans for twelve minutes writes a beautiful half-answer. In practice a great deal of the improvement in a 4ET1 course of study comes from timing discipline rather than literary insight: knowing how long the plan gets, how many paragraphs are realistic, and when to stop improving one point and move to the next. That is trained with a stopwatch, not a textbook.

sections.heading: The components, and what each one is really testing
paragraphs: Families do better when they stop thinking about 'the English exam' and start thinking about the components separately, because each fails differently. The poetry work tests close reading of compressed language and, in the anthology element, the ability to hold two texts side by side without writing two separate essays. The modern prose and modern drama work tests sustained argument across a long text, where the risk is drifting into narrative. The literary heritage element adds older language, which creates a comprehension tax before any analysis can start.

The coursework route matters here. Some centres enter it in place of a written paper, and the experience is entirely different: extended writing produced over weeks, with the school marking against the published criteria. If your child's school has taken that route, a tutor's work is bounded by academic honesty rules that are not negotiable. Feedback on a draft the student has produced is legitimate and useful. Anything beyond that is not, and no reputable tutor will cross that line. Confirm the route with the head of English before planning a term.

The table below sets out the components as a parent needs to understand them — what the student is looking at, what earns marks, and the failure mode each one produces. The exact durations and weightings are published on the current specification at qualifications.pearson.com, and that document is the authority, not this page or any tutor's recollection of a previous version.

One practical note on texts. Because schools choose their own combination from the specification, two Dubai students both sitting 4ET1 in the same series can have no text in common. Any tutor who begins by assuming a text list is guessing. The first email should ask for the exact titles, the anthology poems the department has prioritised, and the entry route.

sections.heading: Unseen poetry: the part students believe cannot be revised
paragraphs: Ask a Year 11 in Dubai which part of the Literature paper worries them and the unseen poem comes up first. The logic seems sound: you cannot revise a text you have not seen. The conclusion is wrong, because what is being assessed is not familiarity with a poem. It is a method, and methods are revisable. A student who has practised the same procedure on thirty unfamiliar poems walks into that question with something to do in the first ninety seconds, which is the whole game.

The procedure we teach is deliberately unglamorous. Read the poem once for sense, without a pen. Read it again marking only two things: where the poem changes direction, and the three words that would be odd in ordinary speech. Write one sentence saying what the poem is doing — not what it is about. Then build three paragraphs, each taking one of those odd words or the shift and saying what it does to the reader. Finish with a sentence on the shape of the whole poem. That is it. It fits in the time the paper allows, and it produces an answer with an argument in it.

What this replaces is the feature hunt. Left to themselves, students who have been taught to identify devices will list them: alliteration here, enjambment there, a metaphor in line six. Each observation is true and each is worth nothing, because the mark scheme asks for effect. Training the procedure breaks the habit by never giving the student a chance to list; the structure forces them to answer 'so what' every time they name something.

Four to six sessions is usually enough to change the score on this element, which makes it the highest-return block in a 4ET1 course of study. We practise on poems from outside the anthology, genuinely unseen on the day, because practising on a poem the student has already discussed teaches nothing about the actual task. Parents often notice the change here before they see it anywhere else on the paper.

sections.heading: The four sentence types, and what band each one reads as
paragraphs: The fastest diagnostic available on a 4ET1 script is to ignore the content and classify the sentences. Students write in recognisable patterns, and each pattern sits in a band almost regardless of which text is being discussed. Once a parent can see those patterns in their own child's writing, the grade stops being mysterious and becomes a list of specific habits to replace. This is the single most useful thing we show families in a first session.

The lowest band is narration: the student tells the examiner what happens. The next is identification: the student names a technique and stops. Above that sits explanation, where the student says what the technique does, usually in general terms. The top band is the sentence that ties a specific choice to a specific effect at a specific moment, and then does something with it — pushes the point, qualifies it, or connects it to a pattern elsewhere in the text. Most students live in bands two and three and believe they are being asked to write more. They are being asked to write differently.

Rebuilding is done one sentence at a time, out loud, with the student's own writing on screen. We take a sentence they produced, name which pattern it is, and rewrite it together into the next pattern up. Three or four of those in an hour is a productive session. After about six weeks the student starts catching the pattern themselves mid-sentence, which is the point at which tuition starts to become unnecessary.

sections.heading: Where 4ET1 marks actually disappear, in order of frequency
paragraphs: Across scripts, the losses cluster in a small number of places, and they are not the places students expect. Vocabulary is rarely the problem. Handwriting almost never is. The big three are question focus, quotation handling and time management, in roughly that order, and all three are mechanical faults with mechanical fixes.

Question focus means answering the question asked rather than the question revised for. A student who has prepared an essay on a theme will produce that essay whatever the paper says, bending the first and last paragraphs to fit. Examiners see this constantly and credit only what addresses the task. The fix is a thirty-second habit: underline the two words in the question that constrain the answer, and write them at the top of the plan. If a paragraph does not touch those words, it does not go in.

Quotation handling is the second. Students are told to use quotations and so they do, dropped in whole lines at a time, parked at the end of a sentence with a colon in front of them. A long quotation costs time to copy and earns nothing extra. Short embedded quotation — two or three words inside the student's own sentence — is faster, reads better and lets the analysis sit next to the evidence. Converting a student from block quoting to embedding often buys five or six minutes on the paper, which is a paragraph.

Time management is the third and the most expensive. A student who writes brilliantly for forty minutes and leaves the second question half-finished loses more marks than any analytical weakness would cost them. We time everything, we practise stopping mid-point when the clock says stop, and we rehearse the unglamorous skill of writing a serviceable final paragraph in four minutes. None of this is literary. All of it is marks.
bullets: Question focus: underline the two constraining words before planning
Embedded quotation of two or three words, never a copied line
A hard stop per question, practised with a clock on screen
A four-minute closing paragraph rehearsed until it is automatic
Nothing left blank: a partial answer outscores an unwritten one

sections.heading: What English Literature tutoring costs in Dubai, in dirhams
paragraphs: Published prices are scarce in this market, which is strange given how much Dubai families spend on tuition. Several of the agencies ranking for these searches quote no figure at all, and two quote in US dollars. The figures below are market rates gathered from providers' own published pricing and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table. They are the market, not an IB Gram price list, and they are included so that a parent can tell whether a quote they have been given is normal.

At the budget end, online tutoring from university students and non-specialist teachers runs from roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour: EdFlik publishes rates from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. A qualified subject teacher working online sits between about AED 150 and AED 300, with Unitors advertising IGCSE tuition from AED 150. An in-home visit, travel included, is commonly AED 180 to AED 500; Bestimate's band is AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors in Dubai reach AED 500. Specialist IB, IGCSE and A Level tutors run AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with TutorChase at AED 270. At the top, BartyED publishes AED 650 for a premium named tutor.

For English Literature specifically there is a hidden variable the rate card does not show: marking. A literature tutor who marks a full timed essay properly spends thirty to forty minutes on it outside the lesson. If that work is included in the hourly rate, the effective cost per hour of the tutor's time is considerably lower than the headline. If it is not included, a parent paying AED 250 an hour for conversation about a text is buying the least valuable part of the service. Ask the question directly before booking: is written marking of timed essays included, and how quickly does it come back?

Context helps too. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package. For a family already carrying fees for two or three children, the tuition decision is usually about how few hours can be made to work rather than how many can be afforded. One well-marked hour a week through Years 10 and 11 beats four unmarked hours in April.

sections.heading: Counting backwards from the Pearson series
paragraphs: Nobody in this market writes about the calendar, which is odd, because the calendar is what decides whether tuition starting in February is useful or decorative. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations are available in May/June and in November each year, and Dubai centres use both. The November series is where resit candidates and private candidates cluster, and its entry deadline falls months before the papers are sat.

The published dates worth knowing are these. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026. November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, including International GCSE November 2027, and those provisional documents can be revised — which is exactly why any date on a tutoring page should be read as a prompt to check the live timetable at qualifications.pearson.com rather than as gospel.

Working backwards from a series produces a plan that looks nothing like 'start tutoring soon'. Set texts need to be finished with reading time to spare, because analysis cannot start while the student is still discovering the ending. Timed essays need to begin early enough that the student has written a dozen before the mocks, not after them. Question-choice strategy is a late job, useful in the final six weeks and wasted in September. And a student considering a November resit needs the entry conversation with the school's exams officer long before the summer results arrive, because the deadline will not wait for a change of mind.

sections.heading: Academic honesty, and the line a 4ET1 tutor holds
paragraphs: English Literature is the subject where the honesty question is sharpest, because the assessed product is writing and writing can be supplied. One operator in this market sells finished assessed work outright. That is not a service with risks attached; it is malpractice, and the consequence falls on the student, whose qualification can be withdrawn. A family paying for it is buying an exposure, not a grade.

The line is simple to state and easy to hold. A tutor may teach the method, discuss a text, question an argument, mark a timed essay against the published criteria and explain why a sentence scored what it scored. A tutor may read a draft the student has produced and say where the argument is thin. What a tutor may not do is supply the sentences that end up on an assessed script. Where a school has entered the coursework route, the school's own rules on outside help are the binding ones and they should be read before tuition starts.

This boundary also happens to be where the teaching actually lives. A sentence handed to a student teaches nothing, because the student cannot generate the next one. A sentence the student rebuilds themselves, with the pattern named out loud, transfers to the next question and the one after. The honest method is the effective method, which makes the choice less agonising than it looks.

The same rule governs materials. Pearson's specifications, past papers and mark schemes are published documents and we cite and link them; we do not reproduce or redistribute them, and a tutor offering a private library of unreleased papers is a reason to walk away rather than a selling point.

sections.heading: Equivalency, option blocks and what Literature is for afterwards
paragraphs: Two questions come up once the immediate grade problem is in hand: does this subject count, and does it lead anywhere. Both have concrete answers in the UAE context, and neither is answered well by the pages currently ranking for these searches.

On equivalency, the UAE Ministry of Education's British-track requirements were clarified publicly in 2026: a student must pass five subjects recognised at GCSE or IGCSE with a grade no lower than E or grade 3, and must show either one subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five. English Literature can sit inside that five, which is worth knowing for a family weighing whether to drop it. One competing page in this market states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects; the sourced figure is five. Equivalency is a Ministry process, not something a tutoring service performs or guarantees, and the authority on it is moe.gov.ae and the emirate's attestation channel.

On where it leads, Literature is one of the few subjects at 16 that is explicitly about handling argument and evidence in prose, which is why it keeps showing up as a preferred subject for law, journalism, politics and international relations. It is also the subject most often dropped at 16 by students who could have done well in it, because a middling IGCSE grade reads as a verdict on ability when it is usually a verdict on method. A student sitting at a 5 because they narrate rather than analyse is not bad at Literature. They have not been shown the sentence yet.

Separately, families should expect the mandatory UAE subjects to run alongside whatever curriculum their school is licensed for. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of curriculum, KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit. That is timetable arithmetic a family should factor in when deciding how many tuition hours an already full week can carry.
